# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXIII. Nell Comes to Grief in an Affair of Honor

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

NELL had to survive for over fourteen days, as things turned out. Nearly four weeks having gone by since the incident with the liniment cake, the time was ripe for her to become involved in a new kind of plight, minor errors—like distractedly pouring a basin of skimmed milk into a container of yarn balls in the pantry rather than into the swine’s trough, and stepping right off the side of the log bridge into the stream while lost in creative daydreaming—not truly being deserving of notice.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0000 }

One week following the afternoon tea held at the manse, a party was thrown by Isolde Pembroke.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0001 }

“Little and choice,” Nell promised Thirza. “Only the female students from our form.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0002 }

A very good time was had by them, and not a single untoward thing took place until tea had ended, at which point they ended up in the Pembroke garden, having grown slightly weary from all their games and ready for whichever tempting type of mischief could show itself. Before long, this manifested as “daring.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0003 }

Taking risks happened to be the trendy pastime for the young children of Brierley at that time. Although it originated with the boys, the trend quickly caught on with the girls, and a whole book could be filled with all the foolish acts performed in Brierley that summer simply because those who did them were “dared” to accomplish them.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0004 }

Initially, Carrie Mott challenged Opal Pettigrew to scale the enormous old willow tree facing the front door up to a specific spot; Opal Pettigrew promptly accomplished this to the embarrassment of the previously mentioned Carrie Mott, despite feeling a deadly terror of the plump green caterpillars swarming the tree and fearing her mother's reaction if her new muslin dress were ripped. Subsequently, Flossie Tulk challenged Odette Pullen to continuously hop on her left leg around the garden, never pausing or placing her right foot down; Odette Pullen bravely attempted this feat, but her strength failed at the third corner, forcing her to admit defeat.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0005 }

Because Flossie’s victory was somewhat more obvious than propriety allowed, Nell Harcourt challenged her to step along the crest of the wooden fence that bordered the garden on its eastern side. Indeed, to “walk” wooden fences demands greater dexterity and balance of mind and foot than a person who has never attempted it might imagine. However, Flossie Tulk, though lacking in certain traits that foster popularity, possessed at minimum an innate and inherent talent, properly practiced, for stepping along wooden fences. Flossie navigated the Pembroke fence with a light indifference that appeared to suggest that such a small feat was not deserving of a “dare.” Unwilling praise met her achievement, as the majority of the remaining girls could respect it, having endured much adversity themselves during their attempts to step along fences. Flossie stepped down from her elevated spot, glowing with success, and shot an adversarial look toward Nell.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0006 }

Nell flipped her red braids.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0007 }

“I do not consider treading on a small, low, wooden fence to be a particularly impressive feat,” she remarked. “In Marysville, I was acquainted with a girl capable of balancing along the ridgepole of a roof.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0008 }

“I don’t believe it,” Flossie stated flatly. “I don’t believe anyone could walk a ridgepole. At any rate, you couldn’t.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0009 }

“Couldn’t I?” Nell exclaimed impulsively.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0010 }

“In that case, I challenge you to manage it,” Flossie stated with defiance. “I challenge you to scale that spot and balance across the ridgepole belonging to the kitchen roof of Mr. Pembroke.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0011 }

Nell grew pale, yet the sole course of action was obvious. She moved in the direction of the dwelling, against whose kitchen roof a ladder rested. Every one of the fifth-class girls uttered, “Oh!” in a mixture of excitement and dismay.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0012 }

“Do not attempt it, Nell,” begged Isolde. “Falling off will kill you. Pay no attention to Flossie Tulk. Daring someone to perform such a perilous act is unfair.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0013 }

“I have to do it. My honor is on the line,” Nell stated gravely. “I will traverse that ridgepole, Isolde, or die trying. Should I be killed, my pearl bead ring goes to you.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0014 }

Nell went up the ladder while everyone held their breath, reached the ridgepole, stood upright and steady on that unsafe perch, and began making her way across it, lightheadedly aware that she was at an uneasy height above the ground and that stepping along ridgepoles was not an activity where your imagination offered much assistance. Even so, she succeeded in making a few strides prior to the arrival of the disaster. At that moment she tottered, slipped from her equilibrium, tripped, lurched, and plummeted, skidding down the heat-dried roof and hurtling off it through the wild mass of Virginia creeper underneath—all preceding the moment when the horrified audience underneath could let out a single, frightened scream.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0015 }

Had Nell tumbled off the roof on the side she had climbed, Isolde would likely have inherited the pearl bead ring right at that moment. Luckily, her fall occurred on the opposite side, where the roof stretched down over the porch so close to the ground that falling from it was far less grave. Even so, when Isolde and the rest of the girls hurried wildly around the building—with the exception of Opal Pettigrew, who stayed as though attached to the earth and collapsed into hysterics—they discovered Nell lying entirely pale and lifeless amid the shattered remains of the Virginia creeper.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0016 }

“Nell, have you been slain?” Isolde screamed as she collapsed onto her knees next to her companion. “Oh, Nell, my sweet Nell, utter merely a single word to me so I know whether you have been slain.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0017 }

It was an enormous relief to every girl, but particularly to Flossie Tulk—who, despite her absence of imagination, had suffered terrible mental images of a destiny marked as the person responsible for Nell Harcourt’s premature and dismal demise—when Nell sat up in a daze and responded hesitantly:
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0018 }

“No, Isolde, I have not been slain, though I believe my senses have been knocked out of me.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0019 }

“Where?” Carrie Mott wept. “Oh, where, Nell?” Nell was unable to reply before Mrs. Pembroke arrived at the location. When she saw her, Nell attempted to haul herself up, only to collapse once more, uttering a brief, keen exclamation of agony.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0020 }

“What is the problem? In what place are you injured?” Mrs. Pembroke asked urgently.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0021 }

“My ankle,” Nell gasped out. “Oh, Isolde, I beg you to locate your father and request that he transport me home. I am certain that walking there is completely beyond me. Furthermore, I am positive I am unable to hop such a distance on a single foot, considering Odette was incapable of hopping even around the garden.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0022 }

Thirza had gone into the orchard to gather a pan of summer apples at the moment she spotted Mr. Pembroke crossing the log bridge and ascending the incline, accompanied by Mrs. Pembroke at his side and an entire train of little girls following behind him. Held within his arms was Nell, her head resting weakly on his shoulder.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0023 }

At that instant, an epiphany struck Thirza. With a sudden burst of dread penetrating her deepest core, she understood the true significance Nell had acquired in her life. She was willing to acknowledge her liking for Nell—indeed, that her affection for Nell was great. Yet, as she rushed frantically down the incline, she now recognized that Nell was more precious to her than any other thing in the world.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0024 }

“Mr. Pembroke, what has happened to her?” she gasped, paler and more unsettled than the composed, rational Thirza had been in a long time.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0025 }

Nell raised her head and gave the response herself.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0026 }

“Do not be too alarmed, Thirza. My tumble happened when I was traversing the ridgepole. My belief is that a sprained ankle has occurred. However, Thirza, a broken neck was a possibility. We should view the situation positively.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0027 }

“When I allowed you to attend that gathering, I should have realized you would do something like this,” Thirza remarked, her relief manifesting as harsh and ill-tempered. “Place her on the couch in this room after you carry her inside, Mr. Pembroke. Good heavens, the girl has swooned!”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0028 }

Indeed, it was true. Unable to bear the agony of her wound, Nell received another one of her desires. She had completely passed out.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0029 }

Directly called away from the harvest field, Obed was immediately sent to fetch the physician, who arrived after a time and found the hurt to be graver than they had believed. The broken bone was in Nell’s ankle.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0030 }

When Thirza went up to the east gable that night, where a girl with a white face was lying, she was greeted from the bed by a plaintive voice.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0031 }

“Do you not feel very sorry for me, Thirza?”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0032 }

“You have only yourself to blame,” Thirza said as she pulled down the window shade and struck a light for the lamp.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0033 }

“Because knowing that I am entirely to blame makes it so difficult, that is the exact reason you ought to feel pity for me,” Nell remarked. “I would feel far better if I were able to place the responsibility on someone else. However, Thirza, what action would you have taken if someone had dared you to walk across a ridgepole?”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0034 }

“I’d have remained on solid, stable earth and permitted them to continue their bold attempts. What foolishness!” Thirza declared.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0035 }

A sigh escaped Nell.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0036 }

“Thirza, you possess immense mental fortitude, whereas I lack it entirely. The prospect of facing Flossie Tulk’s contempt simply seemed unbearable to me. She would have boasted at my expense forever. Besides, Thirza, my suffering has been so severe that you really do not need to be angry with me. Fainting is truly unpleasant, to say the least. Furthermore, setting my ankle caused me terrible agony at the hands of the doctor. Walking will be impossible for me for six or seven weeks, meaning I shall miss the arrival of the new lady teacher. By the time my school attendance resumes, her novelty will have worn off. On top of that, Hughie—and every other classmate—will surpass me academically. Truly, my misfortune is great. Nevertheless, I will attempt to endure every hardship courageously, provided you refrain from being angry with me, Thirza.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0037 }

“Now, now, I am not angry,” Thirza remarked. “You are certainly an unfortunate youngster, without a question; yet just as you mentioned, you are the one who will endure the pain from it. Now then, attempt to consume a bit of supper.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0038 }

“Is it not lucky that I possess this kind of imagination?” asked Nell. “It is going to assist me marvelously, I anticipate. What is done by folks who lack an imagination whenever they fracture their bones, Thirza, in your opinion?”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0039 }

Nell frequently found ample cause to be grateful for her imagination throughout the seven dreary weeks that ensued. Nevertheless, she did not rely entirely upon it. She received numerous callers, and not a single day went by when at least one schoolgirl did not visit to present her with flowers and books, as well as to inform her about everything taking place within Brierley's youth community.
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0040 }

“Everyone has shown so much goodness and kindness, Thirza,” Nell uttered with a happy sigh on the date she was finally able to hobble from one side of the room to the other. “Being stuck in bed is not very enjoyable; nevertheless, there is a positive aspect, Thirza. It reveals to you the true number of friends you possess. Why, I was even visited by Superintendent Bell, who is actually an extremely nice gentleman. Naturally, he is not a kindred spirit; all the same, I am fond of him and feel terribly regretful that I used to find fault with his prayers. I am convinced now that his intentions behind them are genuine, except he has formed the practice of reciting them as though he lacks earnestness. He could overcome that tendency if he would apply a bit of effort. I dropped him a clear, strong suggestion. I explained to him how much I attempted to render my own personal prayers engaging. He recounted to me the entire story of the occasion when he fractured his ankle as a youth. It appears so odd to picture Superintendent Bell as ever having been a child. My imaginative powers have boundaries, after all, because that is something I am unable to visualize. Whenever I attempt to picture him as a child, I picture him wearing gray whiskers and glasses, precisely as he appears during Sunday-school, except tiny. On the other hand, visualizing Mrs. Wace as a young girl is so simple. I have received fourteen visits from Mrs. Wace. Is that not an achievement to take pride in, Thirza? Especially when the spouse of a minister faces so many demands upon her day! Furthermore, she is such a joyful individual to have pay a call on you. She does not ever inform you that you brought it upon yourself and that she trusts you will become a improved girl because of the experience. Mrs. Sowerby invariably remarked that to me whenever she paid me a call; moreover, she stated it in a manner that caused me to sense she might express a wish for me to become a improved girl, yet lacked actual faith that I would. Even Flossie Tulk paid me a call. I treated her with as much politeness as possible, since I believe she experienced regret for daring me to tread upon a ridgepole. Had I perished, she would have been forced to bear a heavy load of guilt for the rest of her days. Isolde has proved to be a devoted companion. She has come across every single day to bring comfort to my solitary bed. However, oh, I will be immensely happy when I am able to attend school, for I have learned such thrilling details regarding the new instructor. All the girls consider her utterly delightful. Isolde states that her light curly hair is the most exquisite, and her eyes are so captivating. Her attire is gorgeous, and the puffiness of her sleeves exceeds that of any other person in Brierley. On every second Friday afternoon, she conducts recitations during which each pupil must recite a passage or participate in a dialogue. Oh, anticipating it is simply wonderful. Flossie Tulk claims to despise it, but that is merely due to Flossie possessing so little creative mind. Isolde together with Opal Pettigrew and Odette Pullen are rehearsing a dialogue, titled ‘A Morning Visit,’ meant for the upcoming Friday. And on the Friday afternoons when recitations are not held, Miss Thorne escorts everyone out to the forest for a ‘field’ day, where they examine ferns, blossoms, and wild birds. Additionally, they perform physical culture routines each morning and afternoon. Mrs. Sowerby claims that she has never encountered such behavior and that the whole thing results from employing a female educator. Nevertheless, I reckon it must be wonderful, and I trust I will discover that Miss Thorne constitutes a kindred spirit.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0041 }

“One matter is clear enough, Nell,” Thirza remarked, “and it’s that your tumble from the Pembroke roof hasn't damaged your tongue in the slightest.”
{: #nw-v01-c23-p0042 }
